title: Battle of Chuncheon (1950): The Defense That Saved South Korea
subtitle: Jun 25 – 30, 1950

lines: Dawn, June 25th, 1950. Rain was falling on Chuncheon, Gangwon Province.
From beyond the 38th Parallel, North Korean shells began to rain down.
The North Korean plan was bold.
Take Chuncheon on day one, then swing southwest and encircle Seoul from behind.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: If it worked, the main South Korean army in Seoul would be trapped within three days.

callouts.text: NK PLAN · SEOUL ENCIRCLED IN 3 DAYS

lines: But the plan began to fall apart on the very first day.
At Chuncheon, a single division stood in the way of an entire North Korean corps.
On the first day of the war, as the front collapsed all along the 38th Parallel,
only one place held: Chuncheon.

visual.text:
Day one of the war —
the only line that held

lines: An underdog defense that bought three precious days.
This is the story of the Battle of Chuncheon, the fight that wrecked the plan to encircle Seoul.

visual.title: Battle of Chuncheon
visual.sub: The Defense That Saved South Korea · 1950

lines: In June 1950, the 38th Parallel was strangely quiet.
With the weekend coming, many South Korean units let their men go on pass and leave.
scenes.label: Seoul streets just before the war (Jun 1950)

lines: The central front around Chuncheon and Hongcheon belonged to the ROK 6th Division.
The 7th Regiment held Chuncheon, the 2nd held Hongcheon, and the 19th waited in reserve at Wonju.
Its commander, Colonel Kim Jong-oh, had been in charge for barely two weeks.
From captured infiltrators and defectors, he sensed that something was wrong.
scenes.label: Kim Jong-oh (later as Maj. Gen., 1954)

lines: Two years later, he would lead the 9th Division at White Horse Hill against China's elite 38th Army.
His first real test came right here, at Chuncheon.
Kim cancelled passes and overnight leave, and put his men on alert.
Trenches were re-dug, and his artillery was pulled in toward the town.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: Chuncheon sits in a basin wrapped by the Soyang River.
North of the river lay the open fields of Oksan-po; south of it, Bongui Mountain, 301 meters high, looked down over the town.
To reach Chuncheon, an attacker had to cross open fields and then the Soyang River.
And every step of that route could be seen from the top of Bongui Mountain.
Facing them was the North Korean II Corps.
Its 2nd Division aimed at Chuncheon, its 7th Division at Hongcheon, led by Soviet-built self-propelled guns.
Under the North Korean plan, II Corps was to take Chuncheon on the first day.
Then it would drive through Hongcheon and Icheon to Suwon, cutting in behind Seoul.

visual.head: OPERATIONS PLAN (SUMMARY)
visual.note: Summary per ROK official history · reconstructed

lines: Dawn, June 25th.
After a thirty-minute barrage, North Korean troops poured across the 38th Parallel.
Breaking through the outposts, the North Koreans rolled onto the Oksan-po fields behind some ten self-propelled guns.
The South Korean soldiers had never seen armored monsters like these.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: Shells fell nonstop among the rain-soaked rice paddies.
The 1st Battalion, 7th Regiment, guarding Oksan-po, faced that armored column with almost nothing.
The South Korean army had no tanks and no real anti-tank weapons.
All it had were 57mm anti-tank guns and a few bazookas.
scenes.label: NK SU-76 destroyed north of Chuncheon (Apr 1951)

lines: The North Korean vehicle was the SU-76.
A Soviet-built armored vehicle carrying a 76mm gun, it looked no different from a tank to the South Korean soldiers.
Then the gunners at Chuncheon made a bold call.
They lowered the barrels of their 105mm howitzers and fired straight at the oncoming guns.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: A howitzer is meant to lob shells over hills.
They turned it into a gun aimed at armor right in front of them.
scenes.label: 105mm howitzer firing (Aug 1950)

lines: And in the middle of the fields, a young officer moved forward.
He was Second Lieutenant Shim Il, an anti-tank platoon leader of the 7th Regiment.

visual.sub: Anti-tank platoon leader, 7th Regt, ROK 6th Division

lines: When shells failed, he and his men crawled toward the guns with grenades and Molotov cocktails.
They reportedly got close enough to drop grenades through the hatches.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: According to official records, his platoon stopped several of the self-propelled guns.
Word that the armored monsters could be destroyed spread quickly along the front.
His feat was later questioned as exaggerated,
but in 2017 a Ministry of National Defense review panel concluded it was true.
On June 26th, the North Koreans tried to cross the Soyang River.
From the top of Bongui Mountain, observers called every North Korean move along the riverbank down to the artillery.
Shells landed exactly where the enemy tried to cross.
scenes.label: ROK divisional artillery (Sep 1950)

lines: Under South Korean fire from the heights, the river became a death trap.
Reportedly, only about one company actually made it across.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: Along the riverbank, the North Koreans reportedly left behind the equipment of units that never made it across.
It was the first major setback the North Korean army had faced since the invasion began.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: Remarkably, even a North Korean novel portrays this moment as a defeat.
It says a battalion collapsed within minutes under a storm of unseen bullets.
Meanwhile at Hongcheon, the 2nd Regiment was holding back the North Korean 7th Division.
On the narrow Malgogae pass, North Korean tanks ground to a halt one by one.
Stalled at Chuncheon, the North Koreans changed their plan.
They diverted troops heading toward Inje and poured their firepower onto Chuncheon.
On June 27th, the North Koreans finally crossed the Soyang River.
The 7th Regiment fell back to the Wonchang Pass south of town and blocked the road again.
But by then, the western front had already collapsed.
On June 28th, Seoul fell.
scenes.label: NK tanks entering Seoul (Jun 1950)

lines: After taking Seoul, the North Korean army halted there for three days.
Some historians argue it was because II Corps, which was meant to close the trap, had not yet arrived.

visual.sub: When the North Koreans did not cross the Han

lines: To avoid being cut off, the 6th Division now had to pull back.
It did not collapse; it withdrew south in good order.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: Even after losing Hongcheon on June 30th,
the 6th Division fought its way back toward Wonju and Chungju, and kept itself together as a fighting unit.
So how did one division hold up an entire corps?
Let's break it down into four factors.
First, they were ready in advance.
One decision to cancel passes meant the 6th Division's men were at their posts that morning.
Many other units were caught half-empty.
Second, the river and the mountain.
Open fields, the Soyang River, and Bongui Mountain.
The attackers had nowhere to hide, while the defenders could see everything.
Third, artillery firing over open sights.
An army without anti-tank weapons used its howitzers as anti-tank guns.
Massing the artillery at Chuncheon paid off at the decisive moment.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: Fourth, the men who held to the end.
According to the U.S. Army history, the North Korean 2nd Division lost about 40 percent of its strength.
Within days of the invasion, North Korea had to replace its corps and division commanders.

visual.note: NK 2nd Division losses · per U.S. Army history (Appleman)

lines: Even Shtykov, the Soviet ambassador in Pyongyang, described the causes in his report:
rugged terrain, and the unexpectedly courageous defense of the 6th Division.
More important than any number was the time they bought.
While II Corps was pinned down at Chuncheon, the plan to encircle Seoul from behind fell apart.
Much of the South Korean army was able to escape south of the Han River.
And on that borrowed time, UN forces began arriving in Korea.
It was the first step toward the Pusan Perimeter and the Inchon landing.
scenes.label: Inchon landing (Sep 15, 1950)

lines: The 6th Division's fight did not end at Chuncheon.
A week later at Dongnak-ri, the 7th Regiment ambushed a North Korean regiment and dealt it a heavy blow.
Today, a memorial in Chuncheon honors the battle.
Every June, the city commemorates what Koreans call the 'Great Victory at Chuncheon.'
scenes.label: Chuncheon Battle Memorial Hall

lines: The Soyang River still flows just as it did then.
scenes.label: Dramatization

lines: On the first day of the war, as everything collapsed, one division did not.
What they defended was not just a city, but time for an entire nation.

items.text: One division held as everything collapsed

lines: If this story meant something to you, please subscribe and like the video.
We'll continue to bring the forgotten records of war to light.
